Audit-firm performance therefore provides a more appropriate point of departure for this study than firm performance considered in an unrestricted organisational sense. Organisational performance may also encompass market outcomes and operating effectiveness, but those dimensions do not necessarily carry equal weight when the organisation performs a public-interest assurance function. The distinction narrows the analysis from general commercial success to the relationship between economic sustainability and engagement quality.

The organisational character of auditing has itself changed considerably. Large practices now operate through international networks whose revenues, market reach and specialist resources resemble those of other complex professional-service organisations. The commercial scale attained by the largest international networks illustrates the economic transformation of the profession. Commercial scale, however, does not eliminate the professional-performance problem. Its relevance is instead that very large revenues, extensive market presence and substantial organisational resources do not by themselves guarantee consistently satisfactory engagement execution.

An audit firm that expands its client portfolio but cannot maintain engagement quality may weaken the professional credibility upon which future business depends, while a technically competent practice that cannot develop a sustainable economic base may struggle to finance the people, technology and quality systems required for increasingly complex engagements. The two dimensions are therefore connected without being interchangeable. This tension is visible in North America.

Inspection outcomes in the United States improved over the period reported by the regulator, although deficiencies remained across more than one category of firm (Regulator, 2024). The percentage should not be interpreted as a universal audit-failure rate because the inspection process selects engagements and evaluates particular areas of audit work. The improvement is material, but the coexistence of concentrated market strength and engagement deficiencies illustrates why market share and audit quality should remain analytically distinct.

Canada provides a complementary picture. Regulatory findings likewise indicate variation in engagement execution, but differences in inspection scope and reporting practice limit direct comparison with the United States (Oversight Council, 2024). The Canadian evidence matters here because it shows how a similar market structure can produce a related professional concern without supporting a claim of identical outcomes.

Across Europe, the performance issue is increasingly connected to competition and the ability of challenger firms to absorb more significant engagements. Recent market reports describe a modest redistribution of selected public-interest work beyond the largest networks (Authority, 2023). The increase demonstrates that highly concentrated audit markets are capable of some redistribution. It does not, however, establish that redistribution alone improves audit quality; the argument must still account for capability, investment and engagement execution.
